title: The serpent who kept the precepts
hookLine: the naga prince Bhuridatta keeps the uposatha even when captured (Jataka 543)

lines: A VOW ABOUT ANYONE WHO COMES.
cards: A great snake lies coiled on top of an anthill by a river, perfectly still. He isn't hunting, and he isn't asleep. He's keeping a holy day.

In the Jataka he is Bhuridatta, a prince of the nagas, the serpent beings of the waters, who has come up into the human world to keep the observance without distraction. He has made a vow about anyone who finds him there.

teach.h: THE OBSERVANCE DAY AND HIS VOW.
teach.b: The uposatha is the Buddhist observance day, when lay people take on extra precepts and keep them for the day and night.
Bhuridatta's vow, the story says, is that if anyone wants his skin, his flesh, anything at all, they can take it; he won't break his precepts to stop them. Then the betrayal.
A hunter who knows where he lies betrays him to a snake charmer, in a bargain over a magic jewel. The charmer seizes him and crushes him into a basket.

Bhuridatta has the power to destroy his captor, the story says, with a single angry look. He won't give him even that. He keeps his eyes shut rather than look at the man in anger, so his precept holds.
The charmer drags him from village to village and makes him dance for coins, and still he keeps it.
At last his family searches for him, finds him, and wins him free. Tradition pairs this tale with sila, virtue.
Not a show of goodness for an audience, but a line kept when breaking it would be easy and would even seem fair. The precept isn't tested on a quiet day. It's tested in the basket.

how: On uposatha days, tied to the phases of the moon, Buddhist lay people may visit a temple, listen to teaching, and take extra precepts for the day and night, such as eating no food after midday.

a festival day for feasting and games

p: the naga prince on the anthill

he wouldn't even look at him in anger, so his precept would hold.
the uposatha is an observance day with extra precepts
lay people take them on for the day and night; Bhuridatta came up to keep it undisturbed.
he was too weak to resist
the story says he could have destroyed his captor with an angry look, and chose not to.

games.q: you're Bhuridatta, keeping the observance day. a charmer grabs you. one angry look could destroy him. what do you do?
o: destroy him; he broke the peace, not you.
close your eyes and keep your vow.
games.why: he keeps his eyes shut rather than look at the man in anger, and endures the basket until his family wins him free.

practice: Pick a single precept, like not speaking falsely or not taking what isn't given, and picture the moment today when it will be hardest to keep.
See yourself in that moment, holding the line quietly, the way the serpent kept his eyes closed.

wordCard.voice: Uposatha. The observance day Bhuridatta the naga prince was keeping when, captured and mistreated, he wouldn't even look at his captor in anger. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali uposatha, the observance day Bhuridatta was keeping.

carryVoice: Your line: he kept it. No speech, no drama, just the line, held. Day eight hundred forty-three, done.
